Yes, household and food shopping environments play a significant role in socioeconomic inequalities in fruit and vegetable consumption. 

People from lower socioeconomic backgrounds often have limited access to stores that sell fresh and affordable fruits and vegetables, and may live in areas with a higher concentration of fast food outlets and convenience stores that sell unhealthy foods. This can make it more difficult for them to purchase and consume a healthy diet.

Additionally, households with lower incomes may have limited financial resources to spend on fruits and vegetables, which can be more expensive than processed and unhealthy foods. This can lead to a lower consumption of fruits and vegetables among lower socioeconomic groups.

Therefore, the environment in which people live and shop for food can contribute to socioeconomic inequalities in fruit and vegetable consumption, making it more challenging for disadvantaged groups to maintain a healthy diet.
